Q: How to define discrete dynamic system in the Scilab/Xcos v2024.1.0? A:

I've done this a bunch for custom discrete controllers in Xcos (2024/2025 versions work the same way for this). The scifunc_block_m is perfect for what you want, but you need to handle the flag logic properly so it only updates on the discrete ticks.

Drag a scifunc_block_m from the User defined functions palette into your diagram.

Double-click it and fill the fields like this:

Number of regular inputs: 2

Number of regular outputs: 2

Initial continuous state: leave empty or [] (you don't need it)

Initial discrete state: [0; 0] (or whatever your two initial x(k=0) values are, column vector)

Number of parameters (rpar): 4

Initial firing vector: [] (usually empty)

Sample time (regular & zero-crossing): leave blank here, set it in block properties later

Then hit OK, it'll open the code editor windows one by one. You can leave most blank except the key ones:

In the "Computational function" window (the main one), put the name of your function, e.g. myDiscreteSys

So just one line: myDiscreteSys

Now create a separate file myDiscreteSys.sci somewhere in your path (or exec it before opening Xcos):

function [xnew, y] = myDiscreteSys(flag, x, u1, u2, p1, p2, p3, p4)
  // flag tells Scicos/Xcos what to do
  select flag
  case 1 then  // output calculation (happens every time step)
    // here you compute outputs from current state x and inputs u1,u2
    // example dummy: just forward inputs + some state usage
    y = [x(1) + u1; x(2) * p1 + u2];
    xnew = x;   // no update yet

  case 2 then  // discrete state update (only called on discrete events!)
    // this is where your real dynamics go
    // x is previous state x(k-1), compute x(k)
    xnew(1) = 0.8 * x(1) + 0.5 * u1 + p2 * u2;     // your eq for state 1
    xnew(2) = -0.3 * x(1) + x(2) + p3 + p4 * sin(u1);  // your eq for state 2
    y = [];   // no outputs needed here usually

  case 4 then  // init (optional)
    xnew = x;  // or set initial if needed
    y = [];

  else
    xnew = x;
    y = [];
  end
endfunction

Important: your function must return two things always: updated state vector xnew and output vector y (even if empty).

Back in the block: right-click → Properties (or double-click again if needed) → go to Advanced tab or main tab and set Sample time to your sampling period, e.g. 0.01 (or -1 if inherited, but for pure discrete better explicit).

The 4 params p1..p4 come from context, so in your Xcos context (Setup → Context) define e.g.:

p1=1.2; p2=0.05; p3=3; p4=0.8;

They'll be passed in order.

Test with a simple CLOCK_c connected to an ACTIVATION block pointing to your scifunc_block_m if you want explicit event triggering, but usually just setting sample time is enough for periodic update.

If it doesn't update states, double-check that flag==2 is being hit (you can add disp("update!") inside case 2 to debug in Scilab console).

This keeps everything clean — interface in Xcos, logic in .sci file you can version-control/edit easily.

For more details/examples the official help page is pretty good: https://help.scilab.org/docs/2026.0.0/en_US/scifunc_block_m.html

Good luck, ping if it barfs somewhere!

Q: Python API Rate Limiting - How to Limit API Calls Globally A:

If you truly need a global rate limit (shared across all functions and across multiple processes/hosts), in-memory/decorator-only solutions won’t coordinate — each process keeps its own counter.

A practical way to make it global is to move the limiter state to a shared backend (Redis/PostgreSQL).

One option is Rate Sync: https://pypi.org/project/rate-sync/

Example (global limit shared by all callers)

[stores.redis]
engine = "redis"
url = "redis://localhost:6379/0"

[limiters.api]
store = "redis"
rate_per_second = 1.0   # 1 request / second globally
max_concurrent = 1

from ratesync import acquire
import requests

def call_vendor_api(url: str):
    with acquire("api"):  # shared across functions/processes/hosts
        return requests.get(url)

Now it doesn’t matter whether x() or y() (or multiple workers) call the API — they all go through the same global limiter.

Q: From which package do I import @WebMvcTest in Spring Boot 4.x? A:

Yes, you are doing the import correctly. The location org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.WebMvcTest is the right package to import. Also, spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test is the correct Spring Boot test starter to bring it in.

As indicated in the comments, the problem encountered during test execution might have a different reason.

Q: How to launch browser in full screen (maximised)- playwright c# A:

make ViewportSize = ViewportSize.NoViewport as below, this will launch browser perfectly in maximised mode

using IPlaywright playwright = await Playwright.CreateAsync();

IBrowser browser = await playwright.Chromium.LaunchAsync(new() { Headless = false, Args = new List<string> { "--start-maximized" } });

IBrowserContext context = await browser.NewContextAsync(new() { ViewportSize = ViewportSize.NoViewport});

IPage page = await context.NewPageAsync();

Q: Best Practices for Handling API Rate Limits in Python Applications A:

If you need global coordination across processes/servers, one option is Rate Sync:

https://pypi.org/project/rate-sync/

[stores.redis]
engine = "redis"
url = "redis://localhost:6379/0"

[limiters.vendor_api]
store = "redis"
rate_per_second = 5.0
max_concurrent = 2

from ratesync import acquire
import asyncio
import httpx
import random

async def call_api(url: str, payload: dict):
    async with acquire("vendor_api"):  # global rate+concurrency gate
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as c:
            r = await c.post(url, json=payload)

    if r.status_code == 429:
        retry_after = r.headers.get("Retry-After")
        if retry_after:
            await asyncio.sleep(float(retry_after))
        else:
            # basic backoff + jitter
            await asyncio.sleep(1.0 + random.random())
        return await call_api(url, payload)

    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

This keeps retries and throughput stable and compliant, even when you scale out to multiple workers.
